action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 5.8 nmol/L and blocking antibody 41%; MuSK not detected; normal thyroid function.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: New fatigability, diurnal variation, bulbar and proximal weakness in a woman labelled CPEO: AChR antibodies are the first test and would overturn the label (Jacob 2025; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 16% in orbicularis oculi, 13% in nasalis and 11% in deltoid without facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: With AChR binding 5.8 nmol/L and blocking 41% the diagnosis is serological, so neurophysiology is good practice rather than necessary (ABN makes it mandatory when antibodies are negative); a decrement also confirms a junctional disorder, which mitochondrial myopathy does not cause (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MRD1 improves by 4 mm on each side after 3 minutes of ice, where it was negative at the first evaluation.
action_criteria.label: Perform an ice pack test on the ptotic lids
action_criteria.rationale: A bedside test of neuromuscular ptosis; a now-positive result after a negative one is the change that reopens the CPEO label.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; fatty involution of the thymus.
action_criteria.label: Order contrast CT (or MRI) of the mediastinum
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with AChR-positive MG, by CT or MRI, and the result informs the thymectomy decision (Jacob 2025; ICG 2020). Renal function is normal for contrast with metformin.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 2.6 L (87% predicted, 32.9 mL/kg), MIP -58 cmH2O, MEP 74 cmH2O: normal.
action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity and mouth pressures
action_criteria.rationale: She now chokes on liquids, a significant bulbar symptom, and has fatigable proximal weakness; baseline vital capacity, mouth pressures and cough decide the level of monitoring before immunotherapy, which can transiently worsen MG (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm 72/min; PR 162 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 412 ms; no conduction defect.
action_criteria.label: Record a baseline 12-lead ECG before pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: ABN asks for an ECG before pyridostigmine, the more so with a topical beta-blocker that adds bradycardia; a normal conduction system also counts against Kearns-Sayre syndrome (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Topical timolol is absorbed systemically, is a beta-blocker caution in MG and adds bradycardia with pyridostigmine; prostaglandin analogues are alternatives.
action_criteria.label: Check her timolol eye drops against myasthenia
action_criteria.rationale: Ophthalmic beta-blockers are easily overlooked and can aggravate MG; considering a switch of the glaucoma treatment is a concrete management change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in orbicularis oculi.
action_criteria.label: Order single-fibre EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Not needed once RNS shows a decrement and AChR antibodies are positive.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic nuclear or mitochondrial variant in blood.
action_criteria.label: Order a mitochondrial gene panel
action_criteria.rationale: Only if doubt about coexisting CPEO remains after the MG work-up, for example a poor response to treatment of the fixed ophthalmoparesis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No ragged-red fibres, no excess of COX-negative fibres for age and no mtDNA deletion on long-range PCR of muscle: no mitochondrial myopathy.
action_criteria.label: Order a muscle biopsy with mitochondrial studies
action_criteria.rationale: Acceptable but not needed for the MG diagnosis: it is the test that settles a coexisting mitochondrial myopathy, because single mtDNA deletions are often confined to muscle and are missed by blood genetics.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not start prednisone at full dose (for example 1 mg/kg daily) at once; escalate from a low dose, because steroid initiation can transiently worsen MG (Jacob 2025).
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or mitochondrial (CPEO) cause before AChR antibody testing (and neurophysiology when serology is negative).
required_recommendations: Revise the diagnosis to new-onset AChR-positive generalized MG superimposed on the long-standing ptosis and ophthalmoparesis, and explain to the patient and her ophthalmologist that a coexisting mitochondrial myopathy is not excluded (a muscle biopsy would settle it if the fixed ophthalmoparesis does not respond); long-standing ophthalmoparesis may respond only partly to treatment.

Ask ophthalmology to consider replacing timolol drops with a non-beta-blocker glaucoma treatment, such as a prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) or a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, because beta-blockers, including ophthalmic ones, are used with caution in MG (ICG 2020).

Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily after a baseline ECG, with heart-rate watch while she uses timolol drops, titrating to effect (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily); the maximum is 360 mg/day, with specialist review above 300 mg/day (Jacob 2025).

If symptoms persist on pyridostigmine, start prednisone 5-10 mg daily and increase by 5 mg every 3-5 days to 30 mg daily (up to 1 mg/kg, not above 60 mg, only after specialist discussion), warning that weakness may worsen around days 5-10, with closer glucose monitoring and adjustment of her diabetes treatment (Jacob 2025). Start azathioprine early alongside the steroid, after TPMT (and NUDT15 where available) testing, because her diabetes and BMI of 30.9 raise the risk of steroid toxicity (Jacob 2025; Fionda 2026).

Before long-term immunosuppression: an ophthalmological assessment before high-dose steroids, given her ocular hypertension; HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure and weight before steroids; hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) and hepatitis C serology, TB screening (IGRA) and HIV test; vaccinations updated at least four weeks before (Jacob 2025; Fionda 2026). During steroids: periodic blood pressure, glucose, weight and eye checks, calcium and vitamin D, and bone densitometry (Fionda 2026).

Discuss thymectomy once MG is optimally controlled: ABN 2025 advises discussion at 50-65, early (within about two years of generalized onset, which here was 8 months ago), while ICG 2020 recommends it at 18-50 and found no benefit at 50 or over in the post hoc MGTX analysis; there is no thymoma on CT, and the expected benefit is less certain if her long-standing ptosis was myasthenic.
Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment because she chokes occasionally on liquids (Jacob 2025).
Record the MGFA class (here IIb) and a baseline MG-ADL, with QMG where available, to follow treatment against the goal of MG-ADL 0-1 (Fionda 2026; Jacob 2025).

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG does not inform ptosis or bulbar weakness.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); normal reflexes and gait give no reason to look for Miller Fisher syndrome.
FDG-PET has no place in the work-up of MG or CPEO.
No cardiac symptoms or murmur; the ECG shows no conduction defect.
Normal PR and QRS on the ECG and no syncope or palpitations; no conduction question to monitor.

ABN reserves brain and orbit MRI for suspected MG with negative serology and neurophysiology; with AChR antibodies positive and no long-tract or other brainstem sign, it answers no question, and extraocular muscle atrophy does not separate long-standing MG from CPEO (Jacob 2025).
Her fatigable hip flexor weakness is documented on examination and gait is normal; a timed gait and balance battery is not part of the MG work-up (Jacob 2025).

Her fatigable muffled voice is documented on examination; a motor speech and language battery does not assess swallowing, which her choking on liquids calls for (a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment) (Jacob 2025).

accepted: New-onset AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis (MGFA class IIb) superimposed on long-standing ptosis and ophthalmoparesis previously labelled CPEO; a coexisting mitochondrial myopathy is not excluded without muscle biopsy

differential.diagnosis: Coexisting chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (mitochondrial myopathy)
differential.key_features: Decades of progressive ptosis and fixed ophthalmoparesis fit CPEO, but new fatigability, diurnal variation, a now-positive ice pack test, an RNS decrement and AChR antibodies establish MG; normal lactate and CK. A coexisting mitochondrial myopathy is not excluded by blood genetics, because single mtDNA deletions are often confined to muscle; muscle biopsy, if obtained, shows no mitochondrial pathology.
Ptosis with dysphagia and proximal weakness fits OPMD, but onset at 20, no family history, fatigability, decrement and AChR antibodies point to MG.
No ataxia, no conduction defect on the ECG, onset at 20 without systemic features.
Ophthalmic beta-blockers can aggravate MG but do not cause AChR antibodies or decades of ptosis.
Decades-long ocular presentation, preserved reflexes, no post-exercise facilitation, AChR antibodies positive.
No proptosis or lid retraction, no Graves history, normal TSH and free T4.

key_clinical_evidence: Ptosis since age 20 labelled CPEO, with eight months of new fatigability, diurnal variation, diplopia, bulbar fatigue, choking on liquids and fatigable hip flexor weakness.
Ice pack test now positive (4 mm each side) after a previously negative test.

AChR binding 5.8 nmol/L and a 3 Hz decrement in facial and deltoid muscles: new-onset AChR-positive generalized MG; the CPEO label is reopened, and a coexisting mitochondrial myopathy is not excluded without muscle biopsy.
Timolol eye drops are a beta-blocker caution in MG (used with caution, ICG 2020); ophthalmology should consider a non-beta-blocker alternative.

No thymoma on CT; thymectomy is to be discussed at 53 (ABN advises discussion at 50-65; ICG 2020 found no benefit at 50 or over), with less certain benefit after a long ocular history; her diabetes and BMI of 30.9 call for closer glucose control and an early steroid-sparing agent.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: New fatigability, a now-positive ice pack test, an RNS decrement and AChR antibodies overturn the label.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior clinical diagnosis of CPEO with a negative ice pack test at the first evaluation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the CPEO label and pursue a mitochondrial work-up; miss MG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Orbital MRI is not indicated here; if obtained, its extraocular muscle atrophy also occurs in long-standing MG and does not distinguish the two.
red_herrings.data_point: Mild reduction of extraocular muscle volume on orbital MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the muscle atrophy as confirmation of a myopathic CPEO.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Topical timolol is absorbed systemically and is a beta-blocker caution in MG; ask ophthalmology to consider a non-beta-blocker alternative such as a prostaglandin analogue.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Overlook a topical medicine as innocuous.

sequence_constraints.reason: RNS is the initial neurophysiological test; SFEMG is considered when RNS is normal and suspicion persists, where expertise is available (Jacob 2025).
Serology comes first: with positive AChR antibodies SFEMG is rarely needed, while every antibody-negative patient needs neurophysiology, RNS first and SFEMG where expertise is available (Jacob 2025).

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: prior CPEO diagnosis creates anchoring bias; new fatigability and positive ice pack test are the pivotal clues; timolol eye drops as hidden contributing drug-disease interaction
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required tools, 3 red herrings; label-revision case with an anchoring prior diagnosis and a hidden drug-disease caution
metadata.revision_reason: Diagnosis worded as new-onset generalized MG on long-standing ptosis and ophthalmoparesis with a coexisting mitochondrial myopathy not excluded; optional muscle biopsy with a stored report; neurophysiology recommended and respiratory function required; mediastinal MRI accepted; baseline ECG before pyridostigmine; sourced SFEMG constraint reasons; timolol replacement as a consideration, pyridostigmine maximum, outpatient steroid titration with early azathioprine, screening with ophthalmology before high-dose steroids, ABN and ICG thymectomy discussion and MG severity recording in the management; waste labels for brain and orbit MRI, the gait battery and the speech battery

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping of decades duration initially diagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — now worsening with new fatigability

family_history: Mother had hypertension and type 2 diabetes; no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease; no family history of similar ocular disease
past_medical_history: Elevated intraocular pressures (ocular hypertension), managed with timolol eye drops
Prior clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)

social_history.note: Teacher; married with three adult children; non-smoker; no alcohol; originally from Ghana, resident in UK for 18 years

patient.history_present_illness:
A 53-year-old Ghanaian woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral eyelid ptosis and increasing generalized fatigue. She first noticed left upper eyelid drooping at approximately age 20, which gradually worsened over years and was eventually followed by bilateral ptosis. She reported no diplopia, diurnal variation, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness throughout this time. She had multiple prior evaluations, and the consistent clinical picture (gradual onset without fatigability, no diplopia, absent ice pack test response at initial evaluation) led to a clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Over the past 8 months, however, she noticed new and different symptoms: significant fatigue with prolonged talking or chewing, muffled voice quality that was worse in the afternoon, and difficulty completing her usual 30-minute walk due to bilateral leg fatigue. She also experienced occasional choking with liquids. She noted for the first time that the eyelid drooping seemed more pronounced when tired and somewhat better in the morning, a pattern she had not observed before. She also reported a sensation of double images on lateral gaze, which resolved with eye closure.

Her ocular history included bilateral elevated intraocular pressures (managed with timolol eye drops) and bilateral cataract surgery 3 years prior (significant improvement in acuity post-operatively). She had no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease. On examination, complete bilateral ptosis was present. Restricted extraocular movements were present, more pronounced in vertical gaze. A new finding was fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation, absent in prior evaluations.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Restricted extraocular movements in all directions, more so in vertical gaze. Diplopia on extreme lateral gaze. Fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation (new finding). Pupils equal and reactive. No tongue fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Limb strength 5/5 in upper limbs. Hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable on sustained resistance). No fasciculations.

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild central adiposity; no organomegaly
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman; alert and cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible immediately; pseudophakic in both eyes, no proptosis or lid retraction. Weight 79 kg, height 160 cm.
physical_exam.neurological: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Extraocular movements restricted in all directions, more so in vertical gaze; no pain on eye movement. Diplopia elicitable on extreme lateral gaze but not in primary position. Fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation (new finding). No tongue fasciculations. Limb strength: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable), otherwise 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. Cerebellar examination normal. Sensation intact throughout. Gait normal.
